nodes.name: 04extra_minimal_race_condition_with_lock.py
nodes.summary: Minimal demonstration of a race condition fix using threading.Lock, where 10 threads increment a shared global counter safely inside a critical section.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a module-level global counter and a threading.Lock acquired/released around the critical section to serialize access across 10 concurrent threads.

nodes.name: increment
nodes.summary: Increments a shared global counter max_val times, guarding each increment with a lock acquire/release to avoid a race condition.

nodes.name: 05_multi_threaded_pool_lock.py
nodes.summary: Demonstrates ThreadPoolExecutor with a shared Lock to safely aggregate a common counter and list while four threads each sum a partition of a large range.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor and wait() to collect futures; a shared Lock protects COMMON_COUNTER and COMMON_LIST mutated from multiple threads.

nodes.name: my_sum_mod
nodes.summary: Sums integers in [a, b) and, for multiples of m, safely updates a shared counter and list under a lock; returns the partial sum.

nodes.name: 06_multi_threaded_pool_queue.py
nodes.summary: Demonstrates ThreadPoolExecutor combined with a thread-safe queue.Queue as an alternative to explicit locking for collecting values found by concurrent worker threads.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses queue.Queue.put()/get() as an inherently thread-safe structure, avoiding the need for a manual Lock used in the sibling 05_ script.

nodes.name: my_sum_mod
nodes.summary: Sums integers in [a, b) and pushes multiples of m onto a shared thread-safe queue instead of using a lock; returns the partial sum.

nodes.name: 07_multi_processing.py
nodes.summary: Basic example of true parallelism using multiprocessing.Process, spawning two separate OS processes that each sum half of a large integer range concurrently.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses multiprocessing.Process.start()/join() directly rather than a pool, illustrating the most basic sub-process API and bypassing the GIL entirely.

nodes.name: my_sum
nodes.summary: Sums integers in the range [a, b) and prints the result; used as the target function for each spawned process.

nodes.name: 08_multi_processing_pool_starmap.py
nodes.summary: Demonstrates multiprocessing.Pool.starmap to distribute a range-sum computation across 4 worker processes with a blocking call that returns all results at once.
nodes.languageNotes: starmap is a blocking pool API that unpacks tuples of arguments into the target function, contrasting with the non-blocking starmap_async used in script 09.

nodes.name: my_sum
nodes.summary: Sums integers in the range [a, b), prints, and returns the result; distributed across a process pool via starmap.

nodes.name: 09_multi_processing_pool_starmapasync.py
nodes.summary: Demonstrates the non-blocking multiprocessing.Pool.starmap_async API, polling readiness in a loop while sub-processes compute partial sums in the background.
nodes.languageNotes: starmap_async returns immediately and exposes .ready()/.get(), letting the main thread continue other work until results are needed, unlike the blocking starmap in script 08.

nodes.name: my_sum
nodes.summary: Sums integers in the range [a, b), prints, and returns the result; distributed asynchronously across a process pool via starmap_async.

nodes.name: cpu_intensive.py
nodes.summary: Sequential baseline for a CPU-bound Monte Carlo integration benchmark, running 10 chunks of a numerical integration one after another without any concurrency.
nodes.languageNotes: Serves as the timing baseline compared against the threaded and multiprocessing variants of the same computation, useful for illustrating the GIL's effect on CPU-bound workloads.

nodes.name: f
nodes.summary: Arbitrary mathematical function sin(1/(x*(2-x)))^2 used as the integrand for the Monte Carlo integration.

nodes.name: cpu_function
nodes.summary: Performs a seeded Monte Carlo integration of f(x) over 2 million random samples and returns the hit count and sample size.

nodes.name: cpu_intensive_threading.py
nodes.summary: Runs the same CPU-bound Monte Carlo integration as cpu_intensive.py but distributes the 10 chunks across a ThreadPoolExecutor, illustrating that threading provides no speedup for CPU-bound work due to the GIL.
nodes.languageNotes: Directly comparable to cpu_intensive.py and cpu_intensive_multiprocessing.py to contrast sequential, threaded, and multi-process execution times for the same CPU-bound task.

nodes.name: f
nodes.summary: Arbitrary mathematical function sin(1/(x*(2-x)))^2 used as the integrand for the Monte Carlo integration.

nodes.name: cpu_function
nodes.summary: Performs a seeded Monte Carlo integration of f(x) over 2 million random samples and returns the hit count and sample size; submitted as a task to a ThreadPoolExecutor.

nodes.name: cpu_intensive_multiprocessing.py
nodes.summary: Runs the same CPU-bound Monte Carlo integration as cpu_intensive.py but distributes the 10 chunks across separate processes, demonstrating real parallel speedup for CPU-bound work by bypassing the GIL.
nodes.languageNotes: Directly comparable to cpu_intensive.py and cpu_intensive_threading.py; multiprocessing achieves true parallelism for CPU-bound tasks where threading cannot due to the GIL.

nodes.name: f
nodes.summary: Arbitrary mathematical function sin(1/(x*(2-x)))^2 used as the integrand for the Monte Carlo integration.

nodes.name: cpu_function
nodes.summary: Performs a seeded Monte Carlo integration of f(x) over 2 million random samples and returns the hit count and sample size; distributed across worker processes.

nodes.name: io_intensive.py
nodes.summary: Sequential baseline for an I/O-bound benchmark that downloads a list of remote image URLs one at a time and saves each to disk under a content-hashed filename.
nodes.languageNotes: Serves as the timing baseline compared against the threaded and multiprocessing I/O variants, illustrating that threading (unlike for CPU-bound work) does help I/O-bound workloads since the GIL is released during blocking I/O.

nodes.name: io_function
nodes.summary: Fetches a remote file over HTTP, computes an MD5 hash of its content for the filename, and writes the file to the local pics directory.

nodes.name: io_intensive_threading.py
nodes.summary: Runs the same I/O-bound URL-fetching benchmark as io_intensive.py but distributes the downloads across a ThreadPoolExecutor, showing that threading speeds up I/O-bound work because the GIL is released during blocking network calls.
nodes.languageNotes: Directly comparable to io_intensive.py and io_intensive_multiprocessing.py to contrast sequential, threaded, and multi-process execution times for the same I/O-bound task.

nodes.name: io_function
nodes.summary: Fetches a remote file over HTTP, computes an MD5 hash of its content for the filename, and writes the file to the local pics directory; submitted as a task to a ThreadPoolExecutor.

nodes.name: io_intensive_multiprocessing.py
nodes.summary: Runs the same I/O-bound URL-fetching benchmark as io_intensive.py but distributes the downloads across separate processes, used to compare process-based vs thread-based vs sequential I/O concurrency.
nodes.languageNotes: Directly comparable to io_intensive.py and io_intensive_threading.py; for I/O-bound tasks, multiprocessing typically offers no advantage over threading but carries higher process-creation overhead.

nodes.name: io_function
nodes.summary: Fetches a remote file over HTTP, computes an MD5 hash of its content for the filename, and writes the file to the local pics directory; distributed across worker processes.

nodes.name: docker-compose.yml
nodes.summary: Docker Compose configuration standing up a standalone Spark cluster with a spark-master, one or more scalable spark-worker containers, and a Jupyter notebook client, exposing the Spark UI, master port, and notebook interface.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses prebuilt images (jpazzini/mapd-b:spark-master/worker/jupyter) and depends_on ordering so workers and the Jupyter client wait on the master; SPARK_WORKER_CORES/MEMORY env vars tune per-worker resources and the service can be horizontally scaled with --scale spark-worker=N.

nodes.name: spark-master
nodes.summary: Spark cluster master node acting as the head node and resource manager, exposing the Spark master UI on port 8080 and the cluster RPC port 7077.

nodes.name: spark-worker
nodes.summary: Spark worker node that connects to spark-master and provides processing capacity, configurable via SPARK_WORKER_CORES and SPARK_WORKER_MEMORY, and scalable to multiple replicas.

nodes.name: jupyter-notebook
nodes.summary: Jupyter notebook service bundling the Spark client and Python interpreter, exposing the notebook UI on host port 1234 and the Spark application UI on port 4040.

nodes.name: README.md
nodes.summary: Guide for the PySpark module explaining the Docker-based cluster setup (master, worker(s), Jupyter client), how to start/scale/stop the cluster, and a summary of the topics covered in Lectures 1-3 (core Spark, DataFrames, structured streaming).

nodes.name: Lecture1.ipynb
nodes.summary: Introductory PySpark notebook covering connecting to a Dockerized Spark cluster, creating a Spark Session and Spark Context, basic RDD operations (parallelize, map, reduce), the Spark application Web UI, word count, computing pi via Monte Carlo, and a distributed gradient descent exercise.
nodes.languageNotes: Large exercise notebook (115 cells) that introduces the SparkSession/SparkContext entry points and core RDD transformations/actions before moving to DataFrames in later lectures.

nodes.name: Lecture1_solutions.ipynb
nodes.summary: Solutions companion to Lecture1.ipynb, providing completed implementations of the Spark Session setup, RDD operations, word count, pi estimation, and distributed gradient descent exercises.
nodes.languageNotes: Mirrors the structure of Lecture1.ipynb but with worked-out answers, intended as an instructor/reference copy of the exercise notebook.

nodes.name: Lecture2.ipynb
nodes.summary: PySpark DataFrames notebook covering Spark SQL, creating DataFrames from Rows, tuples, and Pandas DataFrames, basic DataFrame operations, and User Defined Functions (UDFs) and Pandas UDFs.
nodes.languageNotes: Builds on the SparkSession introduced in Lecture 1 and shifts focus from low-level RDDs to the higher-level, schema-aware DataFrame/Spark SQL API, including UDF and PandasUDF interoperability with Pandas.

nodes.name: Lecture2_solutions.ipynb
nodes.summary: Solutions companion to Lecture2.ipynb, providing completed implementations of DataFrame creation, DataFrame operations, and UDF/PandasUDF exercises.
nodes.languageNotes: Mirrors the structure of Lecture2.ipynb but with worked-out answers, intended as an instructor/reference copy of the exercise notebook.

nodes.name: Lecture3.ipynb
nodes.summary: Spark Structured Streaming notebook demonstrating stream processing by reading from a TCP socket source (populated by the producer.py script) and applying distributed streaming transformations to the incoming records.
nodes.languageNotes: Introduces Spark Structured Streaming's model of treating a continuous stream as an ever-appending table, and relies on the companion producer.py script as the external TCP data source.

nodes.name: Lecture3_solutions.ipynb
nodes.summary: Solutions companion to Lecture3.ipynb, providing completed implementations of the TCP socket streaming source setup and distributed stream processing exercises.
nodes.languageNotes: Mirrors the structure of Lecture3.ipynb but with worked-out answers, intended as an instructor/reference copy of the exercise notebook.

nodes.name: producer.py
nodes.summary: Standalone TCP socket server that generates randomized fake transaction records (name, surname, amount, delta_t, flag) as JSON lines and streams them to a connected client, used as the data source for the Lecture 3 Structured Streaming exercises.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a raw socket.socket() server (bind/listen/accept) rather than a framework, and argparse to accept the hostname to bind to; supplies the socket source consumed by Lecture3.ipynb / Lecture3_solutions.ipynb.

nodes.name: send_messages
nodes.summary: Continuously generates a random transaction-like JSON message and sends it, newline-terminated, over the given client socket every 0.2 seconds until interrupted or the socket errors out.
